scenes.text: Spring shift at the satyr bar: new travellers and the first busy tables of the season.
Summer shift at the satyr bar: the room stays loud late into the evening and service never really slows down.
Autumn shift at the satyr bar: festival traffic and demanding guests turn routine service into crowd management.
Winter shift at the satyr bar: fewer strangers, more regulars, and longer conversations around warm tables.
Spring arrival rush: you triage wet cloaks, fresh orders, and new travellers without letting one table capture the whole floor.
Spring table reset: you reorganize the room between waves, keeping service moving while staff and guests compete for the same narrow space.
Summer split order: two crowded tables merge requests into one noisy list, and you keep the service sequence clear without promising special treatment.
Summer refill rush: heat and evening traffic keep every tray in motion, so you coordinate refills and staff handoffs instead of racing alone.
Autumn queue control: festival guests argue over priority, and you state the service order calmly enough that the room keeps moving.
Autumn closing reset: after the festival wave, you coordinate cleanup, missing cups, and the next shift's setup before the doors finally quiet.
Winter familiar order: regular patrons know the routine, but recognition stays professional and does not become a promise of private access.
Winter hearth round: a smaller room means every delay is visible, so you balance familiar requests, staff pacing, and the last supply checks of the night.

actions.label: Undead Farm shift
actions.description: Work a shift on the undead farm. This is the first target production layer; final wage/stat tuning remains balance-owned.

scenes.text: Spring farm shift: wet ground, fresh growth, and ordinary planting work define the day.
Spring runoff forces you to choose what can be planted now and what needs drainage first.
As process keeper, you separate ordinary spring output from anything unstable before it reaches storage.
Summer farm shift: fast growth and heavy maintenance make ordinary output abundant.
Summer overgrowth turns the shift into triage between harvest volume and worker maintenance.
Keeper-level summer work is a production run: sort the high-volume crop before the heat spoils it.
Autumn farm shift: harvest and processing compete for storage space and time.
Autumn work shifts toward sorting stable goods that can actually survive delivery.
As process keeper, you reserve part of the autumn output for reliable supply instead of pushing everything out at once.
Winter farm shift: storage, repair, and strange preserved materials move indoors.
Winter storage exposes a small unstable specimen that needs separation from ordinary stock.
Keeper-level winter work turns the indoor bench into a controlled specimen and storage station.

actions.label: Tavern shift
actions.description: Work an ordinary tavern shift. Initial wage/stat tuning remains balance-owned.

scenes.text: The roads reopen after winter, and the common room fills with people seeing unfamiliar faces for the first time in months. Their boots carry mud and their maps are crossed with abandoned detours; your job is to learn quickly who needs a meal, who needs a dry place for their gear, and who only needs a clear answer about where the road runs now. Warmer weather brings more guests who have never stayed here before. They ask about house rules, nearby roads, and safe places for their luggage, and you notice how much more useful a calm explanation is than a confident answer to something you do not actually know.

A spring shift runs between ordinary service and small repairs: plaster is drying in one corner, a door sticks in another, and one guest room is temporarily closed while its shutters are fixed. You warn travelers early and rearrange the work without promising more space than the house can actually provide.

The first caravans arrive in uneven groups: one wagon is late, another reaches town before its guide, and a third only wants a place until dawn. Speed matters less than passing accurate information between the hall, rooms, and yard so nobody inherits someone else's promise.

In summer, tables empty and fill again before the dishes have time to cool. You track sequence rather than faces: who is only waiting for companions, who needs a room tonight, and who is already leaving for the next pass.

By evening, demand for rooms grows faster than the supply of free keys. You cannot create space with words, so you track which rooms are actually ready, which beds are already promised, and where an alternative should be offered while the traveler still has time to choose it.

A group returning from a long route brings dust, rolled maps, and too many versions of the same road. You separate requests for water, food, and rooms from route stories so useful information does not disappear into fatigue and boasting.

In autumn, nearby tables discuss supplies, return routes, and fair schedules all at once. You make sure an order note does not turn into a rumor and an overheard conversation does not become a promise made on behalf of the house. Festival guests bring cases, cloth, performance lists, and confusion about lodging. You do not try to run the festival itself; your part is making sure people know where their belongings are, when a room becomes free, and who they should ask next.

By the end of the shift, several ordinary supplies run out earlier than expected. You do not invent a new price or promise an impossible delivery; you record what remains, offer an available substitute, and tell the next shift exactly what needs checking in the morning.

Hunters return with wet cloaks, signs of the forest road, and a habit of speaking briefly. They need space for gear, hot food, and a clear answer about what can be left in a common room and what should stay with its owner.

Winter closes a road faster than travelers can revise their plans. Several guests who expected to leave in the morning now need to stay longer, and your job is to check rooms, food, and shared-space boundaries again without turning an involuntary delay into someone else's debt.

In a cold week, it matters more than usual to know what is actually in storage and what only exists in an old note. You check the real stock and warn the hall before an ordinary request can become an argument.

A messenger brings word that part of the road is closed, and the room's conversations change within a minute. You do not pretend to be a road authority; you record the source, state what is confirmed, and refuse to present an anxious guess as fact.

actions.label: Hunter shift
actions.description: Complete an ordinary local hunting job without entering the 2-Energy expedition layer. Initial tuning remains balance-owned.

scenes.text: A thaw-season local contract stays close to the city edge: confirm the sign, finish the paid task, and return before a short job turns into an expedition.
Meltwater has crossed several track lines. You compare stride, depth, and broken crust so fresh movement is not confused with marks widened by runoff.
The spring trap-check is maintenance work: inspect the line, free a bad catch safely, reset only what is usable, and report damage instead of extending the job into a pursuit.
Recognized spring work means scouting muddy edge approaches, marking washed crossings, and handing the next shift a route note that distinguishes passable ground from an expedition problem.
A summer escort is ordinary paid work: pace the marked route, check water stops, keep the client inside the agreed line, and return before heat turns a local job into a larger hunt.
Training work stays practical. You read bent brush and disturbed dust, explain which sign is reliable, and end the exercise while there is still enough daylight for a clean handoff.
Fresh predator sign near the settled edge calls for verification, not a dramatic chase. You confirm direction, warn the client route, and leave a clear boundary for any later expedition.
Autumn handoff days are busy with ordinary returns. You sort tags, field notes, and usable trophies so each contract stays attached to the right place, time, and client.
A tracker shift follows migration sign only far enough to update the local map. You separate seasonal movement from unusual disturbance and bring the distinction back for the next contract.
A recognized handoff is less about display than provenance: match the specimen or trophy to its route notes, identify what is ordinary, and flag only the evidence that might justify rarer work.
Winter daylight is too scarce to waste on guesswork. A short local track-check confirms what moved recently, what is old sign, and which route can be worked without gambling the whole day.
Recognized winter work is route triage: mark what remains passable, what needs a Rope Kit, and what should wait for a properly prepared two-Energy expedition.

actions.label: Guard patrol
actions.description: Work an ordinary guard patrol or city-duty shift. Initial tuning remains balance-owned.

scenes.text: Spring duty begins with meltwater, damaged roads, and renewed boundary disputes. Ordinary Guard work is to hear both sides, keep passage usable, and record what actually happened without turning every disagreement into a use-of-force scene.

In a yard, fence, or passage dispute, the useful questions are concrete: where the marker stood, who used the road, and what changed after winter. The Guard records both accounts and separates verifiable details from demands.

A road reopened after winter quickly fills with repair crews, trade carts, and travelers. The shift is about establishing a clear passage order and handing the next patrol a record of damage and temporary limits.

Summer festival duty means lost property, overloaded lanes, and people who cannot hear ordinary directions through the noise. The Guard keeps narrow routes open and resolves small disputes before the crowd amplifies the pressure.
A good summer shift is visible in whether people know where to go and what is happening. Short instructions repeated consistently to several groups reduce pressure better than performative threats.

In a hot market, conflict often begins with a queue, a blocked passage, or mismatched expectations rather than a crime. Professional duty restores safe movement first and then handles the underlying complaint.
Autumn brings more cargo, passes, and written marks to the gate. The Guard checks discrepancies against documents and facts rather than treating uncertainty as proven guilt.

A suspicious pass is a reason to check date, seal, route, and cargo description. If the details match, detention is not an end in itself; if they do not, the discrepancy should be recorded so another person can verify it.

By the end of a trade day, memory is already unreliable. A written report links the complaint, the pass, and the actual shift decision so the next review does not depend on rumor or a participant's status.

Winter patrols face closed roads, scarce beds, and people caught between shelter and movement through the city. Poverty is not a crime category; the job is to keep usable access open and record the actual problem.

When people gather near cheap lodging or on the street, professional duty requires distinguishing a dangerous blockage, ordinary lack of space, and someone who simply has nowhere to go. One condition should not automatically imply another.

A closed quarter needs clear detours, supply awareness, and consistent instructions for different groups. Threats do not create order by themselves; it is more useful to state what is closed, why, and which route remains available.

actions.label: Merchant shift
actions.description: Work an ordinary market, appraisal, delivery, or negotiation shift. Initial tuning remains balance-owned.

scenes.text:
After winter the market does not reopen all at once: some stalls are active while others are still waiting for deliveries. You compare promised timing with what actually arrived and do not treat early demand as guaranteed profit.

The spring road is open again, but washouts make an ordinary delivery less predictable. You confirm an arrival window in advance and give the buyer a clear margin of time instead of making an impressive promise.

The first large spring lot looks promising until the records show a difference between the manifest count and what reached the stall. You reconcile the notes first and only then discuss the next trade.

A summer crowd creates fast demand, but not every buyer wants the same thing. You ask short questions about timing and needed quantity so a busy market does not turn into a chain of random concessions.

In the heat, some goods cannot be held indefinitely. You mark what must move today, what can wait until tomorrow, and what should not be promised at all when delivery already falls outside a safe window.

At the stall, people argue about price, timing, and condition at the same time. Instead of offering one broad discount, you separate the questions: one buyer needs a date, another needs lot condition, and another needs clear return terms.

Autumn abundance looks uniform only from a distance. You compare lots by condition, storage time, and supplier reliability without assuming that a large harvest automatically makes every purchase worthwhile.

Before the cold season, storage notes matter more than an attractive display. You separate goods that can safely be held longer from those better sold or returned earlier, and record the reason.

Two suppliers offer similar lots, but one reliably keeps timing while the other promises more volume without confirmation. You compare not only the offer but also the history of meeting obligations.

In winter, scarce goods quickly draw a queue, which is exactly why you do not treat scarcity as proof of any price. You record available quantity, promises already made, and buyers who need predictable supply.

A closed stretch of road changes an ordinary delivery: some orders can be delayed, some split, and some are better cancelled honestly. You explain the constraint before the delay turns into a dispute.

With limited stock, regular buyers ask for their usual quantity. You clarify actual needs and distribute commitments so scarcity does not become a contest of loud promises.

actions.label: Artist House shift
actions.description: Work an ordinary rehearsal, performance, or guest-facing Artist House shift. Initial tuning remains balance-owned.

scenes.text:
A spring shift begins by returning to fundamentals: entrance, pacing, space, and agreement with a partner. The novelty of the season does not replace rehearsal; it only changes what the audience and coworkers notice.

Spring brings more unfamiliar guests to the Artist House, and ordinary work means reading the context of the evening quickly. You welcome people and explain the program without turning attention to a guest into a promise of personal intimacy.

Before a new program, it helps to leave a short note: what changed since the last rehearsal, what needs repeating, and what the next partner should know. The note supports the work rather than creating a separate art-rating system.

A summer evening makes performance more open and noisy: people arrive later, conversations take longer to settle, and the room fills more quickly. You keep the shape of the piece and preserve clear transitions between stage and guests.

In the hot season, a strong piece depends less on who stands out most and more on who listens to a partner and changes pace at the right moment. You leave room for another entrance and do not turn a shared scene into a contest for attention.

When there are many guests, attention has to be distributed rather than held at any cost. You close one conversation gently, hand the guest to the next part of the evening, and preserve the house rhythm without a hidden favor meter.

In autumn, ordinary shifts more often sit beside preparation for public events. You check costume, entrance order, and a fallback without assuming that the existence of a festival automatically makes a performance prestigious or victorious.

A bolder stage presence remains a chosen professional technique. It does not imply agreement to every expectation from an audience, guest, or coworker and does not remove the right to change presentation in the next piece.

After a busy evening, you review concrete moments: where an entrance was missed, where a conversation ran long, and where the scene became clearer. The review helps the next shift without becoming a universal talent or reputation rating.

A winter shift takes place in a tighter salon setting where a pause, a phrase, and a response to one person are easier to notice. You work with more precision, but the intimacy of the room does not become special social status.

When there are fewer events, it is easier to see what makes a program sustainable: repeatable preparation, clear notes, and partners who know the order of work. You use the quiet season to improve ordinary work rather than trigger an automatic career leap.

In winter, familiar guests more often return with established expectations. You remember the context of earlier evenings, but each new conversation remains separate: prior attention creates no permanent promise or mandatory personal route.

actions.label: Assassin shift
actions.description: Complete an ordinary covert work shift such as surveillance, delivery, route preparation, or cleanup. Initial tuning remains balance-owned.

scenes.text: Spring work follows changing crowds and newly busy routes: observe what shifted, verify the handoff context, and keep a fallback if the plan no longer fits.
Long light and crowded streets make timing less predictable. The shift rewards patient observation, clear handoffs, and the willingness to abandon a bad window.
Routes and routines change with the season. Compare what was expected with what is actually happening before deciding how to finish the ordinary assignment.
Short light and formal indoor traffic change what can be seen and when. Keep the task bounded, confirm the context, and close the records when the work is done.

endings.title: Своя в артели
endings.description: Пять практик, практичность 6 и выполненный заказ. Наследие: ночлег за половину цены и практичность +5 на старте.
endings.epilogue: Артель вручает вам ключ от комнаты. Орвин предлагает отпраздновать вдвоём и тут же уточняет, что котёл на этот раз приглашения не получил. Можно согласиться на первое свидание или оставить вечер дружеским. В следующей жизни вас встретят как свою.

endings.title: Дипломированная алхимичка
endings.description: Сдать экзамен. Наследие: смекалка +5 на старте и один бесплатный урок каждую неделю.
endings.epilogue: Диплом пахнет чернилами и слегка — карамелью. Взрослый выпускник соседней мастерской приглашает вас на праздничный ужин: «Без пробирок, обещаю». Свидание остаётся вашим выбором, а право на новое начало уже заслужено.

endings.title: Хозяйка третьего тоста
endings.description: 18 смен в таверне. Наследие: обаяние +5 в следующей жизни.
endings.epilogue: Ваша доля в таверне закреплена договором. Марек приглашает отметить это ужином вдвоём; дружеский вечер тоже его вполне устраивает. Домом иногда становится место, где знают, как вы любите чай.

endings.title: Праздник без разрешения
endings.description: Защитить самостоятельность городского праздника. Наследие: чуткость +5.
endings.epilogue: Горожане выбирают вас распорядительницей праздника. Марек оставляет два места на крыше — полюбоваться огнями, поговорить или наконец выспаться.

endings.title: Приглашение под печатью
endings.description: Передать накладную принцу. Наследие: дерзость +5.
endings.epilogue: Принц вручает вам придворное приглашение с улыбкой, рассчитанной на памятник. Статус вырос; мелкий шрифт ещё предстоит изучить. На празднике вы сами выбираете компанию.

endings.title: Бригадир поневоле
endings.description: 24 смены у лесорубов. В следующей жизни дневной запас энергии +1.
endings.epilogue: Бронн вручает вам ключи от артели и свисток. «Главное — свистеть до падения дерева». Вы остаётесь руководить работой на своих условиях.
